stories.title: Law Firm Greenberg Traurig Takes 25K SF at Related Ross Dev in West Palm
stories.excerpt: Law firm Greenberg Traurig is relocating to another Related Ross building in Downtown West Palm Beach, Fla. The firm signed a 10-year lease to occupy about 25,000 square feet at the 15 CityPlace office development, which remains under construction, the tenant announced. The deal spans the entire 12th floor of the 25-story project. Move-in is scheduled for fall 2027. “The move reflects our long-term commitment to the West Palm Beach market and positions us to meet increasing client demand throughout Palm Beach County and beyond,” Tracy Gerber, co-managing shareholder of Greenberg Traurig’s West Palm Beach office, said in a statement. 15 CityPlace, and the neighboring 10 CityPlace, are expected to be completed next year after developer Related Ross secured a $772 million construction debt package last year. Health care provider Cleveland Clinic has already pre-leased 125,000 square feet at 15 CityPlace, which will span about 500,000 square feet. The law firm is currently stationed at Philips Point, where it leases roughly 30,000 square feet. Related Ross, led by Stephen Ross, purchased the 448,914-square-foot office for $282 million in 2021. The two-building complex, which dates back to 1985, is currently undergoing a $120 million renovation. Even as Greenberg Traurig departs, the building has nabbed new tenants: global index provider MSCI taking 7,500 square feet, investment bank Solomon Partners taking 4,200 square feet, and Integrity Pro Consulting taking 1,300 square feet. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Greenberg Traurig signs 10-year, 25K SF lease at Related Ross's 15 CityPlace, West Palm Beach; move-in fall 2027.
Cleveland Clinic pre-leased 125K SF at same tower; $772M construction financing secured last year.
Law firm cites 'increasing client demand throughout Palm Beach County' as driver of long-term commitment.
stories.summary: Greenberg Traurig is relocating within Downtown West Palm Beach, committing to 25,000 SF on the 12th floor of the under-construction 15 CityPlace tower through 2037. Cleveland Clinic has already pre-leased 125,000 SF at the same 500,000 SF mixed-use project. Related Ross closed $772M in construction debt last year, and the building is on track for delivery in 2025.
stories.impact: Major professional service and healthcare anchor tenancies signal sustained business and professional services demand in West Palm Beach CBD, validating dense office/mixed-use development economics. This reduces lease-up risk for Related's 15 and 10 CityPlace and suggests strong underlying demand for Class A multifamily in adjacent West Palm Beach markets as white-collar workers and medical professionals relocate.

stories.title: Law Firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee Leases 11K SF at 7 World Trade Center
stories.excerpt: Washington D.C.-based law firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee is establishing a new office in New York City. The firm, which specializes in high stakes trials, investigations and crisis management, has inked an 11,167-square-foot lease on the 34th floor of 7 World Trade Center, developer and landlord Silverstein Properties announced Monday. Silverstein did not disclose the length of the lease or the asking rent. However, a source close to the deal noted asking rents in the building range from $100 to $150 per square foot. “We are excited to welcome our teams and our clients into our new Manhattan office later this year,” Jeannie Rhee, managing partner of Dunn Isaacson Rhee, said in a statement. “7 World Trade Center offers the ideal combination of thoughtful design, functionality, and a premier location in the heart of the Financial District and a stone’s throw to the Southern District of New York courthouse.” Dunn Isaacson Rhee will relocate from 11 Park Place, also in the Financial District. It’s unclear when the firm will make the move. Dunn Isaacson Rhee did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Lisa Ann Pollakowski, Cory Gahr and Richard Plehn from Lee & Associates represented the tenant in the deal, while Silverstein was represented in-house by Keith A. Cody, Gordon Hough and Harlan Strader, as well as by CBRE’s MaryAnn Tighe. Lee & Associates did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. “Dunn Isaacson Rhee represents the caliber of organization that continues to define 7 World Trade Center as one of Downtown Manhattan’s premier office destinations,” Silverstein’s Cody said in a statement. “Today’s leading firms are seeking workplaces that reflect their brand, support their people and provide an exceptional experience for their clients. bullets: D.C.-based law firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee leases 11,167 SF on 34th floor, 7 World Trade Center, Manhattan.
Asking rents $100–$150/SF in building; firm relocating from nearby 11 Park Place in Financial District.
Firm cited 'premier location' near Southern District courthouse as key to NYC expansion.
stories.summary: Washington D.C.-based litigation firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee is opening a new Manhattan office with an 11,167 SF lease at Silverstein Properties' 7 World Trade Center in the Financial District, moving from 11 Park Place. Asking rents in the building range from $100–$150/SF, and the firm will occupy space later this year.
stories.impact: Legal and professional services flight from D.C. to NYC Financial District reflects continued strength in Manhattan's financial and litigation services ecosystem. Silverstein's tower infill and tenant momentum indicate robust office leasing velocity in Lower Manhattan, reducing structural office-to-residential conversion pressure and supporting underlying demand for workforce housing in nearby Brooklyn and Queens submarkets.

stories.title: Alliance for Downtown New York Inks 14K SF at 42 Broadway
stories.excerpt: Nonprofit group Alliance For Downtown New York has expanded its Lower Manhattan footprint to 42 Broadway. The Downtown Alliance, which manages the area’s business improvement district, secured a 14,420-square-foot lease at the Financial District tower, according to a recent CBRE office market report. The Downtown Alliance plans to relocate its operations division to the 22-story office building, a spokesperson for the nonprofit told CO. The nonprofit’s corporate headquarters remain housed roughly three blocks north at Silverstein Properties’ 120 Broadway. JLL’s John Wheeler and his team at JLL represented the tenant in the negotiations. A spokesperson for the team did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The lease terms were not disclosed, but office asking rents in Lower Manhattan averaged $61.91 per square foot in July, according to the CBRE report. A spokesperson for the landlord, Avi Schron‘s Cammeby’s International Group, confirmed the recent transaction to CO, adding that the space is still under construction. It was not immediately clear whether Cammeby’s International Group worked with any outside brokers. Cammeby’s 42 Broadway is located near the intersection of Broadway and Morris Street. Appellate service organization Office of the Appellate Defender relocated there in November, joining a tenant roster that includes office suite provider TKO Suites, chiropractor Prestige Health and Wellness, dental practice DDS Group and cafe Gregorys Coffee. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Alliance for Downtown New York (BID manager) leases 14,420 SF at 42 Broadway, Financial District.
Relocating operations division from headquarters 3 blocks north; Lower Manhattan office rents averaged $61.91/SF in July.
Space still under construction; lease terms not disclosed.
stories.summary: The nonprofit Alliance for Downtown New York, which manages the Lower Manhattan BID, has signed a 14,420 SF lease at Cammeby's International Group's 42 Broadway to relocate its operations division. The building is a 22-story Financial District office tower. Lower Manhattan office asking rents averaged $61.91/SF in July; specific lease terms were not disclosed.
stories.impact: Low relevance to multifamily development. BID relocation signals continued institutional stability and reinvestment in Lower Manhattan's office stock, but does not materially affect apartment demand, supply, or capital allocation in regional markets.

stories.title: New York’s Rent Freeze Was Only An Aftershock. This 2019 Law Was The Quake.
stories.excerpt: Jose Tur owns two rent-stabilized rental buildings in Manhattan’s Washington Heights with a total of 45 units. The properties have been in his family for over 30 years, and the mortgages are fully paid off. But Tur tells Commercial Observer that despite this, while he’s reluctant to give an exact number, “more than two or three” units have been sitting empty for an average of over two years. That’s because, according to Tur’s estimates, it would cost anywhere from $30,000 to $60,000 per unit to return them to a livable state, and that’s money he can’t justify spending in return for the stabilized rent amounts in today’s environment. “Some of them require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Tur, who has testified about these financial challenges to New York City’s Rent Guidelines Board (RGB). “[Oftentimes] the plumbing’s really old because a tenant has lived there for 10 to 15 years, and you have to do the electrical and then lead abatement, which really increases the tally on the job.” Tur says that the $30,000 estimate is before taking into account more cosmetic fixes like cabinets, tiles and so forth, meaning the total is often closer to $60,000 for a one-bedroom apartment. Given all this, the fate of his currently empty apartments is uncertain. With no financial relief in sight, it is likely the units will not be lived in again for the foreseeable future, removed from the rolls of New York’s livable spaces — and from Tur’s income-producing properties — as if they had never existed. The RGB approved a freeze on rent increases for one- and two-year leases for the city’s rent-stabilized apartments in June for lease terms beginning on Oct. 1 or later. bullets: NYC rent-stabilized owner holds 45 units in Washington Heights; 2+ units vacant 2+ years due to $30K–$60K renovation costs per unit.
2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act capped rents; owner cannot justify capital spend at stabilized rates.
Owner testimony to Rent Guidelines Board highlights widespread capital underinvestment across stabilized stock.
stories.summary: A Manhattan rent-stabilized landlord with 45 units in Washington Heights is leaving multiple units vacant for over two years because renovation costs ($30K–$60K per unit for basic code compliance) exceed returns available under stabilized rent caps. The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act has made it economically unviable for owners to maintain or upgrade units, creating a widening capital maintenance gap across the stabilized portfolio.
stories.impact: Accelerating deterioration of NYC's rent-stabilized housing stock (roughly 1M units citywide) is creating a structural shortage of affordable rental housing and increasing demand for newer, market-rate multifamily development, especially in adjacent outer-borough and suburban markets. Developers should expect sustained rent growth in unregulated markets as stabilized housing effectively exits supply, particularly in Washington Heights, Inwood, and East Harlem.

stories.title: Local Developer Plans to Build a School at 1000 University Avenue in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: School is in session in the Bronx, or at least it will be. Kiumarz Geula, principal of real estate development firm Pillar Property Management, has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to build a seven-story school building at 1000 University Avenue in the Highbridge neighborhood of the Bronx. The plans were filed with the DOB on Aug. 5. Geula did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Jonathan Imani of IMC Architecture, the registered architect on the project, also did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. The DOB plans have few details about the scope of the work coming to the vacant Bronx property. The plans call for the construction of a 64,366-square-foot, 108-foot tall building with a cafeteria and recreation space. No other details are available. Pillar Property Management isn’t the only developer planning to bring a new school building to the Bronx. In June, Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures secured a $60 million debt package to acquire and build a charter school at 1780 East Tremont Avenue, Commercial Observer reported at the time. Ripco Real Estate’s James Murad, who arranged the financing for that deal, told CO at the time that the project reflects “the growing demand for high-quality educational facilities in underserved communities and the continued appeal of mission-driven real estate investments.” Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Pillar Property Management (Kiumarz Geula) filed DOB plans Aug. 5 for 64,366 SF, 7-story school at 1000 University Avenue, Bronx Highbridge.
Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures secured $60M debt for charter school at 1780 East Tremont Avenue in June.
School development pipeline expanding in Bronx; minimal disclosed scope in current filing.
stories.summary: Pillar Property Management has filed plans with NYC DOB to construct a 64,366 SF, 7-story school building at 1000 University Avenue in the Highbridge neighborhood of the Bronx. The project includes cafeteria and recreation space but few other details are available. This follows Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures' June closure of a $60M debt package for a charter school at 1780 East Tremont Avenue.
stories.impact: Accelerating institutional school development in the Bronx (Highbridge and Tremont submarkets) signals capital confidence in the borough's population stability and growth trajectory. Educational infrastructure investment typically precedes and validates multifamily development; developers should monitor both school projects and surrounding residential market rents, as new families and educators relocating to serve new schools drive sustained apartment demand in inner-Bronx and adjacent Westchester spillover markets.
